name: Chess.com
tagline: Online chess platform with matchmaking, ratings, puzzles, lessons and tournaments.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The chess part is genuinely trivial to one-shot: move legality, board UI and a brutally strong engine are all solved, free and open source, and an agent can wire Stockfish to a board in an afternoon. What you cannot generate is ten million people awake at 2am who are rated within 50 points of you. Chess.com's product is matchmaking liquidity, a rating system everyone agrees to care about, a puzzle and lesson library built over years, and anti-cheat that only works at their scale. A local build gives you a sparring partner and a puzzle trainer, which is honestly most of the improvement value, but it is not the same product. If you mainly want to play humans for free, note that a fully open source alternative already exists and is not something you need to build.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you play Stockfish at a chosen strength, step through your mistakes, and grind puzzles from a downloaded puzzle file.
requirements: Stockfish WASM (npm) or a local Stockfish binary
Optional: a downloaded public puzzle CSV for the trainer
Optional: your exported PGN games for review
whatYouLose: Human opponents at your exact rating, on demand, at any hour
A rating that anyone else recognizes or that tracks progress across a real pool
Anti-cheat, fair play enforcement and moderated play
Tournaments, clubs, chat, friend lists and the whole social layer
Structured lesson paths, videos and titled-player content
Mobile apps with cloud sync of games and progress
moatNotes: Rating systems are a coordination good: a number is only worth having if other people accept it. That is not code.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for the paid tiers mostly to remove puzzle and analysis limits and to unlock lessons, but they stay for the pool. Chess is a two-player game and the hard part is the second player: a stranger, awake now, roughly your strength, who will not quit on move nine. Chess.com sells instant access to that plus a rating everyone treats as real, and neither of those is something a local build can fake. The training tooling is the part you can replicate; the opponent supply is the part you cannot.
notes: The trainer is a one-sitting build; the opponent pool is not. The moat is matchmaking liquidity and a rating number that other people have agreed to respect.
prompt:
Build a local single-player chess training app. No accounts, no server-side database, no telemetry, no cloud.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript, client only
- chess.js for rules, move generation and PGN
- react-chessboard for the board UI
- stockfish.wasm running in a Web Worker for the engine
- Zustand for state, localStorage for persistence
- Plain CSS, dark theme, no UI framework

Features in scope:
1. Play a game against Stockfish. Pick color and a strength slider that maps to UCI_LimitStrength / Skill Level plus a per-move time budget. Show a move list, allow undo, resign and new game.
2. Analysis mode: after a game or on a pasted PGN, run the engine over every position at a fixed depth, compute centipawn loss per move, and label moves as good, inaccuracy, mistake or blunder with a simple threshold table. Let the user click any move to jump the board there and show the engine's top line.
3. Puzzle trainer: load puzzles from a local file at ./data/puzzles.csv with columns fen,moves,rating. Serve them in rating order starting near the user's stored puzzle rating, validate the user's move against the solution line, play the opponent replies automatically, and update a local Glicko-ish puzzle rating after each attempt.
4. Local history: store finished games and puzzle attempts in localStorage, with a page showing win/loss record, average centipawn loss over time and puzzle rating over time. Export everything as JSON and as PGN.

Explicitly out of scope: online multiplayer, matchmaking, human ratings, accounts, chat, tournaments, lessons, video, mobile apps, anti-cheat.

Do not bundle any puzzle data yourself. Write a README section telling the user where to drop their own puzzles.csv and note that public puzzle datasets exist under open licenses that they should check themselves.

No .env is needed since there are no secrets. If you add any optional network call later, put keys in .env and gitignore it.

Deliver: working npm run dev, a README with setup in under ten lines, and no dead UI.
